scenario: A 30-year-old G1P0 female at 32 weeks gestation presents with headache, blurred vision, nausea, vomiting, and severe hypertension. She develops eclampsia requiring magnesium sulfate, then apnea requiring ventilatory support and intubation, followed by post-intubation management and antihypertensive therapy.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: What brought you in today, and when did it start?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: What brought you in today, and when did it start?] The utterance is a neutral open-ended intake question with no bad news, blame, loss, or processing burden. Fear stays absent (no clinical threat disclosed), sadness stays absent (no loss), overwhelm stays absent (single simple question), shame stays absent (no judgment or exposure).

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: I've got this bad pounding headache all around my head, and my vision's gone blurry. I've been feeling sick and throwing up, and there's this pain up in the right side of my belly.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Are you pregnant, or could you be? When was your last period?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: Are you pregnant, or could you be? When was your last period?] The utterance is a neutral clarifying question about pregnancy status and last period. It delivers no bad news, no clinical threat disclosure, no complexity burden, and no blame or exposure. Fear stays absent (no new threat conveyed), sadness stays absent (no loss named), overwhelm stays absent (single simple question, not overloading), and shame stays absent (nonjudgmental, routine history-taking).

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: Yes, I'm pregnant, about 32 weeks along. This is my first pregnancy.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Start IV magnesium sulfate now for seizure prophylaxis — she's got severe preeclampsia features at 32 weeks with a BP of 184/120.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Magnesium sulfate is in and running.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Give IV labetalol now — her pressure is severe-range and we need it down to prevent a stroke. Keep the magnesium running.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Your pressure is coming down but still high, so I'm going to keep treating you. Before I give anything else — do you have any drug allergies?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: Your pressure is coming down but still high, so I'm going to keep treating you. Before I give anything else — do you have any drug allergies?] fear absent->present: the utterance conveys her blood pressure remains dangerously high and requires ongoing treatment, an active serious threat to a symptomatic patient, which raises fear; the partial improvement buffers it from escalating further but does not resolve the threat. sadness stays absent: no actual or anticipated devastating loss conveyed. overwhelm stays absent: a single calm update plus one simple question about allergies is not an overload of information or urgent decisions. shame stays absent: no blame, judgment, or exposure - the allergy question is neutral care.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: No, I don't have any allergies to any medications. Please just help me — is my baby going to be okay?

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: I'll be straight with you. Your blood pressure is coming down with the magnesium and labetalol, but it's still high at 156/102. What you have is severe preeclampsia at 32 weeks, and that's dangerous for both you and the baby. The safest treatment is usually to deliver, so I'm bringing in the obstetric team now. I can't promise you the baby will be fine, but we are focused on protecting you both.

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: I'll be straight with you. Your blood pressure is coming down with the magnesium and labetalol, but it's still high at 156/102. messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: Okay... okay, please bring in the obstetric team, do whatever you have to. But this headache is still pounding and my vision's still blurry. I'm still feeling sick, and that pain up in the right side of my belly hasn't let up. Are you sure you're doing everything you can?

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Give another dose of IV labetalol now — her pressure is still severe-range at 160/104 with ongoing symptoms. Keep the magnesium running.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Yes, we're doing everything we can. That pounding headache, the blurry vision, and the pain in your right upper belly are signs the preeclampsia is affecting your organs — that's exactly why we can't wait. The definitive fix is delivering the baby, and the obstetric team is being brought in now to proceed with delivery. In the meantime we're keeping the magnesium running and continuing the blood pressure medication. I won't promise you the baby will be fine, but delivering is the safest option for both of you.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: Okay, do it — go ahead with the delivery, I trust you. But that headache is still pounding and my vision's still blurry. I'm still nauseous, and that pain in the right side of my belly just won't let up.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Give another dose of IV labetalol now — her pressure is still severe-range with ongoing preeclampsia symptoms. Keep the magnesium running.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Good news on one front: your blood pressure has come down into a safer range now, 115 over 80. The magnesium is still running to protect you against seizures. That headache, the blurry vision, the nausea, and the pain in your right upper belly are all from the preeclampsia straining your organs, and they should start to ease once the delivery is done. The obstetric team is going ahead with the delivery now, and that's the definitive treatment for all of this.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: Okay, thank you — I'm glad my blood pressure's come down. But that headache is still pounding and my vision's still blurry. I'm still nauseous, and that pain in the right side of my belly hasn't eased up yet.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: I hear you, and I expected that. That's the organ strain from the preeclampsia, and it only truly lifts once the baby is out. We're watching those symptoms closely, and the obstetric team is proceeding with the delivery right now.
